Subject: Packet priming: TTFT & streaming constraints — follow-up and pilot ask

Hi Megan / Jordan —

Great talk today — thanks for walking through the StratusPay payment-assist flow. Short recap + proposal so we have a clear handoff for a 1-week pilot: 

Key performance targets you mentioned (confirming in our words):
- TTFT (time-to-first-token): <= 150 ms at P95 for user-facing short prompts (priority flows).
- Concurrency: ~200 concurrent live sessions during peak; target steady-state 100 concurrent.
- Sustained throughput: ~40 RPS average, spikes up to 120 RPS for 30–60s bursts.
- Output lengths: avg ~120 tokens, heavy tail to ~600–800 tokens for long receipts/threads.
- Streaming: prefer SSE (server-sent events) for browser clients; WebSocket okay as fallback where SSE is unsupported.
- Chunk cadence: first meaningful token within 150ms; subsequent chunks of 40–80 tokens every ~100–250 ms to keep UX smooth.

What we propose as next steps on our side:
1) Pilot config: 1-week pilot in us-east, dedicated instance pool, canary at 10% gradually ramp to 100% of pilot traffic.
2) Pilot sizing: provisional: 2 dedicated GPU nodes (NVIDIA-class equivalent) with continuous batching + prefix caching.
3) Data needed from you: 1) sample traffic file (anonymous) showing token distribution (we referenced attachment), 2) a short list of 10 representative prompts (edge cases included).
4) Compliance: we'll send SOC2 + data handling brief separately; please confirm any additional evidence you need.
5) Cost/contract: draft pilot MOP attached (sp-pilot-mop.pdf) — we can do a short SOW for the week.

Attachments: stratus_streaming_requirements_v1.xlsx (your sheet), sp-pilot-mop.pdf (Redwood draft), pilot_traffic_sample.json (template).

Questions for you:
- Is the 150ms P95 a hard requirement or a stretch target for the pilot?
- Any client environments where SSE is blocked (older browsers / embedded WebViews)?
- Do you need per-tenant isolation or is a shared-tenant pilot ok with logs/audit access?

If that looks right I’ll loop in Karthik and Laura to size the pilot precisely and propose a canary schedule & rollback plan.

Short and practical — thanks again.

Best,
Ben Carter

Thanks Ben — this is exactly the right level of detail. A few clarifications from our side:

- 150ms P95: this is our consumer-experience goal for the core payment confirmation path. For the pilot, hitting <=150ms P95 on 90% of calls is acceptable (we can iterate).
- SSE: our primary web clients support SSE; some older embedded WebViews in our partner apps require WS — so having both is necessary.
- Isolation: pilot can run in a shared-tenant sandbox as long as we have per-request logs and an audit trail.

We can provide the sample traffic and 10 prompts by EOD Wed (11/11). We also need:
- SOC2 Type II report and a brief on data retention/encryption during the pilot.
- A pilot SLA target (we want to discuss 99.9% availability for the pilot window).

As for the canary, Jordan (cc) suggested starting with 5% traffic for the first day and doubling daily if metrics look good.

Would like an internal sizing note from your infra team (GPU size, estimated VM/node counts, any warm-up steps).

Thanks — looking forward.

Ben / Laura — quick technical readout and questions based on the attached traffic sample template. High level notes: 

Sizing & configuration (provisional):
- Pilot nodes: 2 dedicated inference nodes (NVIDIA H100-equivalent) with 40 GB memory each, continuous batching enabled. This maps to an estimated front-end capacity to meet ~150ms P95 for the average 120-token payload at ~100 concurrent sessions.
- If they intend to run 200 concurrent peaks with the 600–800 token tail frequently, recommend 4 nodes or autoscale with fast-burst capacity.
- Model variant: start with a quantized fp16/8-bit variant of our baseline LLM (recommend small-large tradeoff: fidelity vs latency). We can route long-tail requests to a higher-capacity variant or apply early stopping for non-critical flows.

TTFT and streaming specifics:
- First-token latency: turn off end-to-end token buffering on the server path for the first chunk; use unbuffered immediate flush for the first byte. Continuous batching should be configured with a micro-batch timeout of 8–12 ms to balance batching efficiency and TTFT.
- Chunk cadence: first chunk size = 1–4 tokens emitted immediately (in ~30–60 ms internal time), then emit 50-token chunks with a target inter-chunk interval of 120 ms to match their UX goals. This keeps client-side rendering smooth while minimizing per-token cost.
- Transport: SSE preferred; use WebSocket for embedded WebViews and mobile SDKs that need two-way/cancelable streams. Implement ephemeral request IDs for correlation.

Caching & warm-up:
- Prefix cache: use a 30-minute TTL for high-frequency templates; prefill cache with their top-50 prompts before canary start (we can accept a pre-warm payload from them).
- KV cache: recommend keeping KV cache warm for sessions expected to have multiple turns; TTL depends on session churn but 10–30 minutes is typical.

Observability & canary checks:
- Metrics to gate ramp: TTFT P50/P95, mean token throughput, error-rate, and tail latency for longest requests.
- Canary plan: 5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100% over 4 steps by default, hold for 30–60 minutes at each step; rollback on TTFT regressions >20% or >=0.5% error-rate increase.

Questions for the customer (send back to Megan/Jordan):
- Confirm token distribution (avg / 90th / max) and whether returning to earlier context (multi-turn) is common — that affects KV-cache sizing.
- Any client-side timeout constraints (browser or mobile) we need to honor?

Next steps I propose:
1) We draft a 1-week pilot runbook (will attach) and send a sizing cost estimate.
2) They provide sample payload + top-50 prompts; we pre-warm caches 24 hrs before canary.
3) Run canary and share live dashboard access.

I’ll attach a short pilot_runbook.md and rough cost calc to the internal thread (I’ll post once I convert to PDF).
